subsystems.name: Collector elements
subsystems.role: capture the star's light and convert it to usable energy.

subsystems.name: Orbital architecture
subsystems.role: keeps millions to trillions of independent units in stable, non-colliding orbits.

subsystems.name: Power transfer
subsystems.role: moves captured energy to where it is consumed — beamed, or used locally.

subsystems.name: Material supply
subsystems.role: provides the raw mass; a swarm needs far more material than Earth can launch.

subsystems.name: In-space manufacturing
subsystems.role: builds new collector units from mined material without returning to Earth.

subsystems.name: Replication and control
subsystems.role: lets the swarm grow itself, and coordinates the whole system.

buildSteps.title: Establish in-space industry
buildSteps.detail: First prove that mining, refining and manufacturing can be done off Earth — today only small experiments exist on the International Space Station and a handful of free-flying demonstrators.

buildSteps.title: Seed a factory
buildSteps.detail: Deliver a small, mostly robotic 'seed' factory to a low-gravity body or a stable orbit. It needs little mass because it will build its own successors.

buildSteps.title: Mine a small body
buildSteps.detail: Extract metal, silicon and carbon from an asteroid or from a body like Mercury. Low gravity makes it far cheaper to launch material into orbit than from Earth.

buildSteps.title: Make the first collectors
buildSteps.detail: Roll out extremely thin solar-collecting film — a few grams per square metre — on the simplest frame that survives the space environment. Low mass matters more than efficiency, because the star supplies so much energy.

buildSteps.title: Deploy into many orbits
buildSteps.detail: Release units into a wide range of independent orbits around the star rather than one rigid structure: no known material is stiff enough for a solid shell, and a solid shell would not be gravitationally stable.

buildSteps.title: Replicate
buildSteps.detail: Each generation of machines builds the next, so the number of units can grow exponentially until the collected fraction of starlight becomes large.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Units wear out, so the system must recycle and replace them indefinitely, and manage collisions between trillions of objects.

buildSteps.title: Use the energy
buildSteps.detail: Energy is either used locally for computation and manufacturing, or beamed outward — an enormous engineering challenge in its own right.

prerequisites.why: reusable rockets have cut prices sharply, but a swarm needs millions of times more mass in orbit.
small-scale printing, welding and assembly have been demonstrated, but nothing near industrial volume.
no mission has yet mined or refined material in space at any scale.
the growth of a swarm depends on machines that can copy themselves from local material; this exists only as theory and laboratory-scale work on self-reproducing automata.
power beaming has been demonstrated at small scale in orbit and on the ground, but not at gigawatt-to-terawatt levels.

pathway.milestone: orbital manufacturing demonstrations and asteroid-survey missions
pathway.unlocks: the basic tools and the map of available resources.
structural material that does not have to be lifted out of Earth's gravity well.

pathway.milestone: self-reproducing industrial machines operating off Earth
pathway.unlocks: exponential rather than linear growth in space-based industry.

pathway.milestone: a growing collector array absorbing a measurable fraction of a star's output
pathway.unlocks: energy on a scale that would show up as an excess of infrared light from the star, which is exactly how such a structure would be detected (the idea behind searches for artificial stellar sources).

pathway.milestone: a swarm capturing nearly all of the star's output — a Kardashev Type II civilisation
pathway.unlocks: planetary-scale computation, manufacturing and interstellar capability, if the engineering and social hurdles can be met.
